title: First jobs with Ernest Stevens: park concerts and picnics
summary: His first job was with barber-bandleader Ernest Stevens, playing marches in parks in a big band where he faked his way at about seventeen.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: What was the first job you ever played, even without pay?

Oh the first job I played with a fellow by the name of Stevens, Ernest Stevens, who was from way downtown on St. Claude Street. He was a barber. And on the side he made up little concert groups. And we used to go in the parks and play concerts. That's when I was, oh gee this was so long ago. And then we played some jazz band jobs, you know, no piano, upright bass, horn and drums and trombone and trumpet and clarinet. I played a couple of the dance jobs and then I played in the old Millenburg, a couple of those all day picnics. What did Ernest Stevens play? He played the bass. Also the drums, he played drums or bass.
As a drummer I think he's still alive. Jack Lane told me about it.
He must be very old.
I'm pretty sure he's the one Jack Lane, because all those Stevens guys were drummers.
Well I mean drums was his main fort, you know.
And I played with him quite old, I guess for quite a few months.

And I was trying to learn how to read at the time, that's even before I went to Jufri, you see. Trying to, and I couldn't do so well. And we played in parks like the Bunny Friends Playground and St. Rock Park and those places.
When would that be? What day of the week?
No, I really wouldn't remember. It wouldn't generally be on Sunday.
It could be any day. Not necessarily.
During the night, you know. Oh, nighttime. Night, maybe seven o'clock at night.
What kind of tunes would you play on a job like that?
Old marches. All marches.
And you'd fake your way through all that, huh?
Quite a bit.
Who was in the band, Stevens?
The only one I remember was Stevens. I was just a kid at the time. I believe I was what, seventeen?
Was it a big band?
Oh yeah, it must have been twenty to thirty pieces. Quite a big band, you know, so it covered me up. No matter what I played, nobody knew the difference.
A lot of clarinet players.
Yeah, about three or four, and I probably was the only one who couldn't read. And I'd just fake along whenever somebody else played, I followed.
I see.
